operationalization: Fit outlines and micro-CT surfaces of unilocular tests (Orbulina, Lagena and similar genera) to constant-mean-curvature and sessile-drop profiles, and compare residual error with non-equilibrium shape models. A systematically smaller residual for drop profiles would support the claim; structured residuals concentrated in the neck or aperture would refute a pure fluid-drop equilibrium.

candidate_datasets.name: Endless Forams
candidate_datasets.role: Expert-identified light images of modern planktonic foraminifera, including spherical Orbulina, for outline comparison with a free drop

candidate_datasets.name: AutoMorph Atlantic planktonic foraminifera
candidate_datasets.role: Open 2D and 3D morphometrics and coordinates for tens of thousands of Recent planktonic tests

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Micro-CT volumes of a few foraminifera, including Orbulina, for a three-dimensional curvature check

obstacles: Open 3D coverage is dominated by planktonic Orbulina and Globigerina, while flask-shaped lagenids are mostly represented by plates and SEM images.
A sphere fits many simple generative models, so agreement for Orbulina alone is weak evidence that surface tension set the shape.
rationale: Drop equilibrium is a standard geometric target, and planktonic unilocular tests are already imaged and measured at scale. Those collections barely cover the lagenid shapes Thompson used as the harder cases, and a good geometric fit still leaves calcification timing unmeasured. The comparison can be run on existing images for the planktonic subset within weeks, which is a partial test of the stated scope.

operationalization: Code shell coiling and growth mode for multilocular Foraminifera and for Radiolaria, then test whether exterior accretion predicts a higher frequency of logarithmic spirals. The tendency would be supported by a large excess of spirals among accretionary foraminifera after phylogenetic correction, and weakened if milioline and other accretionary tests are commonly non-spiral at rates similar to non-accretionary skeletons.

candidate_datasets.name: pforams@mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Illustrated taxonomy and morphological characters for planktonic foraminifera

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Micro-CT of foraminifera and radiolaria for comparing spiral and non-spiral skeletons

candidate_datasets.name: Endless Forams
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level images of planktonic tests whose coiling can be scored

obstacles: Exterior accretion is how most foraminiferal tests grow, so the proposed cause is partly built into the materials being compared.
Coiling categories in taxonomic databases are coarse and phylogenetically clustered.
rationale: Spiral versus non-spiral architecture can be scored from existing image libraries, including the radiolarian contrast Thompson draws. The causal step is harder: many shells grow by external addition without becoming logarithmic spirals, and many spirals arise by other routes, so a frequency difference would remain compatible with several growth rules. Available images support a comparative test on well-illustrated groups, not a direct measurement of incremental accretion.

operationalization: Segment septal surfaces from micro-CT of chambered foraminifera and Nautilus, record the sign of curvature relative to the aperture, and compare each septum with the minimal surface spanning the same suture. Support would be outward convexity in foraminifera, outward concavity in Nautilus, and area close to the minimum; a systematic departure toward thicker, non-minimal septa, or curvature unrelated to which side was loaded, would refute the paired claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open micro-CT of foraminifera and cephalopod shells from which septal surfaces can be segmented

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Public CT library including chambered shells suitable for a small septal-curvature sample

obstacles: Public volumetric scans of septate foraminifera and nautiloids number in the tens, not a broad taxonomic sample.
Minimal-area agreement can be produced by several loading histories, so curvature sign is clearer than the pressure story.
rationale: Curvature direction and closeness to a minimal surface are well-defined measurements, and the side the living tissue occupied is known for both groups. The necessary tomographic archives exist but are sparse, so a test would cover a few genera rather than chambered foraminifera and cephalopods at large. Segmentation is routine once scans are in hand, yet assembling a balanced sample would take specialist effort beyond a quick survey.

operationalization: On axial sections and 3D whorls, estimate the spiral angle at successive chambers and test self-similarity by superimposing younger and older outlines after scaling. A logarithmic spiral is supported when the angle is constant and scaled outlines coincide within measurement error; a changing angle, or a better fit by an Archimedean or multistage spiral, would refute it for that shell.

candidate_datasets.name: Fusulinid ontogenetic outlines
candidate_datasets.role: 1,396 digitized whorl outlines from 106 fusulinid specimens, with landmarks at successive growth stages

candidate_datasets.name: pforams@mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Images of spiral planktonic tests for extending the geometric test beyond fusulinids

candidate_datasets.name: bforams@mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Illustrated deep-sea benthic foraminifera, including coiled forms

obstacles: The open landmark series is fusulinid, a subset of the nautiloid and other spiral foraminifera named in the claim.
Trochospiral tests need a 3D angle; equatorial photographs alone underdetermine the spiral.
rationale: Continued similarity is exactly the measurement Thompson uses to recognize a logarithmic spiral, and fusulinid outlines already record shape at each whorl. Image atlases extend the test to many other coiled genera, though not as precomputed spiral angles and not evenly across benthic families. Fitting a constant angle against alternatives is a standard morphometric job on the fusulinid file and a slower image-measurement job elsewhere, so the law is testable now for a large subset.

operationalization: Measure successive whorl breadths on oriented thin sections of Fusulina cylindrica and Fusulina böcki and convert a constant breadth ratio to a spiral angle. The claim is confirmed if the ratio clusters near 1.5 and the angle near 86° across whorls and specimens; a ratio that drifts with whorl number, or a mean far from 1.5, would refute the stated figures.

candidate_datasets.name: Fusulinid ontogenetic outlines
candidate_datasets.role: Whorl-by-whorl outlines for pseudoschwagerine fusulinids and Triticites, a proxy for the expansion ratio in related fusulinids

obstacles: The open coordinate file does not contain the two named Fusulina species.
Published measurements of those species are scattered in monographs and would have to be redigitized from plates.
rationale: The numerical target is unambiguous, so a handful of well-oriented sections could confirm or refute it. What is openly downloadable is an ontogenetic landmark set for related fusulinid genera, which can test whether expansion ratios near 1.5 are typical of that family but cannot substitute for Fusulina cylindrica and F. böcki. Discriminating power is high once those specimens are measured; assembling them is the limiting step.

operationalization: Compute chamber or whorl volume ratios along individual ontogenies and test constancy against a model in which the ratio itself changes with age. A stable ratio matches the geometric pattern; it confirms growth proportional to existing mass only if protoplasmic mass is measured independently and scales with the same constant, which existing hard-part series do not provide.

candidate_datasets.name: Fusulinid ontogenetic outlines
candidate_datasets.role: Successive whorl outlines from which relative chamber size can be calculated through growth

candidate_datasets.name: AutoMorph Atlantic planktonic foraminifera
candidate_datasets.role: Size measurements of individual tests, without chamber-by-chamber growth series for most species

obstacles: A constant size ratio is also produced by other rules, including a fixed volume added in proportion to surface or a fixed developmental schedule.
Living mass at the moment each chamber is added is not in the morphometric archives.
rationale: Relative chamber size through ontogeny is measurable on sectioned and scanned tests, and the fusulinid landmark file is already organized by whorl. The explanatory half of the claim equates that geometric series with mass-proportional growth of a homogeneous body, which shell outlines cannot separate from other constant-ratio mechanisms. The pattern is therefore testable on a subset of chambered forms, and the stated cause is not.

operationalization: For successive chambers, compare observed surfaces with area-minimizing surfaces on the previous aperture, record similarity after scaling, and test whether the contact angle is constant as Rhumbler claimed. The broader account is favored if chambers stay near minimal area and similar in shape even where the contact angle varies; it is weakened if a single contact angle predicts chamber form and minimal-area surfaces do not.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Micro-CT surfaces of multilocular tests for chamber area and contact geometry

candidate_datasets.name: Fusulinid ontogenetic outlines
candidate_datasets.role: Axial outlines through growth for testing chamber-to-chamber similarity

obstacles: Potential energy is inferred from shape, so a minimal-area fit does not measure the forces that acted while the chamber was soft.
Only a small number of chambered species have open volumetric scans.
rationale: The claim sets a minimal-area-plus-proportional-growth account against a narrower constant-angle rule, and both make geometric predictions that sections and scans can score. Energy itself is not observed, and the mapping from a finished calcareous wall back to a soft drop is an interpretation. With sparse 3D coverage, the model comparison is realistic for a few well-scanned genera and illustrative elsewhere.

operationalization: Score planispiral versus trochospiral coiling, ventral flattening, and life habit (attached, free benthic, planktonic) across genera, then test the association with a phylogenetic model. The claim is supported if attached species are disproportionately plane and flattened on the attached face while planktonic species are disproportionately helicoid; abundant attached trochospirals or free planispiral plankton would undermine the stated contrast.

candidate_datasets.name: World Foraminifera Database
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic catalogue of living foraminifera that can be joined to published habit and coiling codes

candidate_datasets.name: ForCenS
candidate_datasets.role: Global surface-sediment census of planktonic species, the floating end of the contrast

candidate_datasets.name: bforams@mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Images and morphological characters for benthic tests, including attached and coiled forms

obstacles: Attached versus free habit and the flattened face are not fields in the census databases and must be compiled from monographs.
Coiling mode is phylogenetically conserved, so a habit correlation can be a clade effect.
rationale: Coiling geometry and life habit are observable and widely described, and planktonic assemblages are already tabulated globally. No single open table pairs attachment, flattening, and coiling across benthic genera, so the test requires a compilation. Exceptions are informative where they have been illustrated, but phylogenetic structure will keep the result from being a clean mechanical demonstration.

operationalization: Compare morphometric clusters with genetic clusters for genera Thompson treats as variable, especially Peneroplis and planktonic groups with many named forms. The claim is supported where single genetic lineages occupy several named species or genera and morphology shifts within a life cycle; it is refuted where those names correspond to stable, reciprocally monophyletic lineages.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public sequences of planktonic and some benthic foraminifera for species-boundary tests

candidate_datasets.name: Endless Forams
candidate_datasets.role: Expert-labeled images of 35 modern planktonic species for comparing named forms with continuous shape variation

candidate_datasets.name: pforams@mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic concepts and images against which genetic clusters can be matched

obstacles: Peneroplis, the example in the text, has far less public genetic and culture data than planktonic globigerinids.
Cryptic species make the opposite error from ecophenotypes, so a single global test will not have one answer.
rationale: Whether named forms are temporary variants or lineages is a standard species-delimitation question, and planktonic foraminifera now have both image libraries and public sequences. Those data cover only part of the benthic diversity the claim invokes, and life-cycle series that would show one individual passing through several 'species' remain scarce. Where sequences and morphology can be paired, the contrast between ecophenotypes and lineages is sharp.

operationalization: Use stratigraphic durations and relative abundances of foraminiferal morphotypes as proxies for persistence and commonness, and ask whether shell-form classes differ in those proxies after sampling correction. Equal fitness would look like indistinguishable durations and abundances across forms; large, repeated differences would count against the claim, without identifying the selective cause.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences from which genus-level stratigraphic ranges of foraminifera can be estimated

candidate_datasets.name: ForCenS
candidate_datasets.role: Modern relative abundances of planktonic species as a coarse commonness proxy

obstacles: Stratigraphic range and abundance are weak stand-ins for fitness and are dominated by preservation and sampling.
Equal persistence is compatible with neutral coexistence, fluctuating selection, and many forms of weak selection.
rationale: The sentence is an inference about fitness from the simplicity of the growth laws, and fitness is not a column in any foraminiferal archive. Ranges and census counts can show whether some shell forms are markedly less persistent or less common than others, which is a partial empirical shadow of the claim. Those proxies would not isolate 'none fitter than another' from sampling bias or from selection that does not change durations.

operationalization: Place shell-shape classes on molecular and stratigraphic trees and count independent origins of the same form. Repeated origins of indistinguishable tests in distant clades or separated time intervals would support the claim; a single origin for each form, with similarity tracking relatedness, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Sequences for building foraminiferal trees independent of shell-shape taxonomy

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence data for asking whether similar forms reappear in disjunct intervals

candidate_datasets.name: pforams@mikrotax
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological and stratigraphic ranges of planktonic taxa to match against trees

obstacles: Many benthic genera are still classified by the shell form whose homology is in question.
Molecular trees are dense for planktonic clades and sparse for the long-ranging benthic groups.
rationale: Independent origin of the same shell is a phylogenetic count, and public sequences plus fossil occurrences make that count possible for planktonic and some benthic forms. Coverage through geological time is uneven, and shape-based taxonomy can manufacture both false convergence and false continuity. The result would be informative where molecules and morphology have both been recorded, and only suggestive for the rest of the order.

operationalization: Compare fragment proportions and shell thickness across assemblages, and test whether more robust forms have higher relative abundance or longer stratigraphic durations. The claim is favored if delicate tests dominate death assemblages with little fragmentation and robustness does not predict persistence; a consistent association of breakage with loss of fragile forms would favor the selective account Thompson rejects.

candidate_datasets.name: ForCenS
candidate_datasets.role: Surface-sediment census counts that record which fragile planktonic species remain abundant as dead tests

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA MD13-3462G foraminifera and grain size
candidate_datasets.role: A core with benthic counts and sediment properties, representative of taphonomic assemblages rather than a breakage experiment

obstacles: Fragments in sediment mix predation, dissolution, compaction, and processing damage.
Abundance of delicate species does not measure whether strength differences affect survival.
rationale: Death assemblages show that fragile tests are routinely preserved, which speaks to Thompson's observation that breakage is not universal. They do not record the selective gradient of strength, and fragment counts are not a standard open variable across the global census. A comparative test can bound how common destruction is, while the evolutionary claim about strength as a guiding advantage stays weakly identified.

operationalization: Regress living and dead foraminiferal abundance on sediment grain size across surface samples, treating grain size as the current-speed proxy Thompson uses. Hydraulic sorting is supported if dead tests track the fine fraction the way other light particles do, including where living animals are present in coarser patches; habitat avoidance is favored if stained living specimens are absent from gravels even when transport is accounted for.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA Elbe Estuary foraminifera and grain size
candidate_datasets.role: Paired living and dead benthic counts with clay, silt, and sand fractions

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA MD13-3462G foraminifera and grain size
candidate_datasets.role: Downcore benthic census joined to siliciclastic grain-size distributions

candidate_datasets.name: ForCenS
candidate_datasets.role: Global planktonic census in surface sediments, to be read against sediment texture where it has been measured

obstacles: Foraminiferal protocols often discard the coarse fraction, so true gravels are under-sampled.
Most open pairs of counts and grain size are regional shelves, estuaries, or single cores.
rationale: The variables Thompson names, test abundance and sediment grade, are published together in multiple open PANGAEA sets, including stained living counts that help separate behavior from transport. Those sets do not constitute a global survey of coarse gravels, and sieving practice biases the record toward mud. A small team can test the association now on the available seafloors, which is a real but geographically restricted resolution of a general sedimentological claim.

operationalization: Predict genetic or stratigraphic relatedness from shell-shape similarity and compare that prediction with one based on molecular characters. The empirical core is supported if shape neighbors are often distant on sequence trees; it is weakened if shape distance remains a reliable predictor of relatedness after the physically forced characters are removed.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Sequences that provide a relatedness measure not defined by shell geometry

candidate_datasets.name: Endless Forams
candidate_datasets.role: Labeled images for quantifying shape similarity among planktonic species

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences for comparing morphological similarity with stratigraphic proximity

obstacles: How much discordance is enough to 'revise the canons' of classification is a judgment, not a threshold in the claim.
Shape-based names enter both the morphological distances and the labels on many sequences.
rationale: The empirical content is that shell similarity is an unsafe guide to consanguinity wherever form is physically determined. Public sequences and image sets can measure that discordance for planktonic foraminifera and, more thinly, for other groups. The further demand to revise classification is a methodological conclusion that the same discordance does not uniquely dictate. The test is therefore informative about convergence and incomplete as a verdict on taxonomic practice.

operationalization: Fit a plane logarithmic spiral to rhinoceros horn sheaths in lateral view and test whether the axis stays in the median plane. A constant angle lying in that plane would support the geometric claim; a helical component, or an angle that changes along the horn, would refute it. The anterior-to-posterior growth ratio is then read from the angle rather than measured as a growth rate.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT and surface scans of rhinoceros skulls, usually of the bony horn base rather than the full keratin sheath

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Museum specimen media, including photographs from which horn curvature can be measured when the sheath is present

obstacles: Keratin sheaths are often removed from skeletal specimens, so scans capture the core and not the curve Thompson describes.
A constant spiral angle implies a constant growth ratio only inside Thompson's growth model.
rationale: A plane logarithmic spiral is a direct fit to a horn outline, and photographs of intact sheaths exist in museum portals. Open 3D coverage of complete rhinoceros horns is thin, and growth velocities at the front and back of the germinal surface are not archived. The geometric half can be checked for the specimens that retain the sheath; the growth-ratio mechanism stays an interpretation of that fit.

operationalization: Reflect one horn of a bovid skull onto the other and measure the residual after alignment. Mirror symmetry is confirmed if residuals are within scanning and wear error across sheep, goats, oxen, and antelopes; a systematic directional asymmetry shared by many species would refute the conjugate-spiral claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Downloadable CT and meshes of bovid crania that retain both horn cores

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Additional museum specimens and photographs spanning Bovidae

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: Public skull CT for a smaller set of ungulates usable as a symmetry check

obstacles: Scans more often preserve bony cores than the keratin sheath, and the sheath carries much of the visible spiral.
Museum holdings over-represent domestic cattle, sheep, and a few hunted antelopes.
rationale: Bilateral mirror symmetry of a pair of horns is a routine landmark or surface comparison, and open cranial scans already include both sides of many bovid skulls. The sample is not a complete survey of every genus, but it is large enough to confirm the general rule or to expose a repeated exception. Wear, injury, and core-versus-sheath differences are measurable nuisances, not barriers to the test.

operationalization: Fit logarithmic, circular, and piecewise spirals to horn centerlines from bovid scans and test whether one angle is constant along the horn. A majority of horns with a stable logarithmic angle would support the geometric claim; a better fit by curves whose curvature changes with length would refute it. Unequal axial growth remains identified with that angle unless increment thicknesses are measured around the base.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D crania and horn cores of hollow-horned ruminants for centerline fitting

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs and specimen records that widen taxonomic coverage beyond scanned skulls

obstacles: Open meshes are biased toward species with skeletal specimens and often lack the keratin sheath.
Constant unequal growth and some adhesion patterns produce the same logarithmic centerline.
rationale: Whether most horns are logarithmic spirals is decidable by curve-fitting on existing scans and photographs, and the methods are standard. The causal clause, a constant ratio of growth on opposite sides, is the geometric meaning Thompson gives the spiral rather than a separate measured growth field. Taxonomic coverage is broad enough for a majority claim about well-collected bovids and incomplete for the family as a whole, and it does not separate growth from later mechanical retardation.

operationalization: Estimate the constant spiral angle of horn sheaths of Oryx, the Sindh wild goat, Ovis ammon, and Highland sheep from calibrated photographs or scans, using the same fitting convention on each. The series claim is confirmed if the angles rise in that order and fall near the stated bounds (under 40°, under 70°, about 75°, and slightly higher); overlap or a reversed order would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D skulls of some Capra and Ovis species for angle measurement

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Museum images of oryx, wild goat, argali, and domestic sheep horns

obstacles: The named forms are not all present as metrically calibrated open 3D sheaths.
Spiral angle on a helical horn depends on how the plane of the generating spiral is chosen.
rationale: The claim is a short ordered list of angles, so it is highly decidable once homologous measurements exist. Museum media cover these animals, but they are not a ready-made morphometric table, and several of the horns are photographed rather than scanned. A small team could measure a modest series from images, with real uncertainty in the angle definition for horns that also twist out of plane.

operationalization: Decompose each argali horn into a logarithmic angle in the generating plane and a helical pitch, then compare Ovis ammon, O. poli, and O. hodgsoni. The claim is supported if the logarithmic angles agree within measurement error while pitch differs; a species difference in the logarithmic angle as large as the difference in pitch would refute the stated partition.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Any open 3D Ovis crania from which spiral angle and helical pitch can be separated

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen photographs of Asiatic wild sheep for a coarser two-view estimate

obstacles: Complete sheaths of all three named argali are scarce in open 3D repositories.
Single photographs confound the in-plane angle with the helical component.
rationale: Separating a shared spiral angle from a differing shear is a well-posed 3D measurement and would cleanly support or reject the comparison among these sheep. Public scans and photographs of the three species are sparse and often show the skull without a full horn, so the test is limited to whatever intact specimens can be assembled. The decision criterion itself is strong; the sample is the obstacle.

operationalization: Around the basal growth zone, map which side of the horn thickened fastest using growth-line spacing or sheath increments, and relate the angular separation of the maximum and minimum to whether the centerline is planar. The claim is confirmed if planarity occurs when those extrema are opposite and a helical component appears when they are offset; it is refuted if planar horns regularly have offset extrema.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Horn-core geometry and, where the sheath is scanned, a surface on which growth bands might be traced

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs showing growth rings on sheep and antelope horns

obstacles: Circumferential growth-rate maps are rarely digitized; most archives store overall shape only.
If the extrema are inferred from the centerline, the test repeats the geometric definition.
rationale: The claim is a geometric rule linking the position of fastest and slowest growth to planarity, and it is testable when growth bands can be read around the horn. Existing 3D archives record the resulting curve much more often than the increment field that is supposed to cause it. A subset of photographed sheaths with clear rings could be measured, but a family-wide test would require new digitizing of increment positions.

operationalization: Measure local attachment or resistance between sheath and core around the growing base, and compare that map with differential keratin deposition and with the resulting curvature. Adhesion would be implicated where curvature matches a measured retardation field in the absence of a matching deposition difference; shape identity of the two mechanisms cannot decide which one acted.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Core geometry of bovid horns; sheath adhesion and growth increments are not recorded

obstacles: Thompson notes that adhesion and unequal growth produce the same spiral, so finished shape does not identify the cause.
No open dataset maps adhesion, membrane attachment, or side-specific retardation during horn growth.
rationale: The claim is that attachment to the bony core can be the chief cause of curvature, and that this cause imitates unequal growth. Public scans can show that core and sheath differ in curvature, which is consistent with sheath-level shaping, but they contain neither adhesion nor deposition rates. Because the two mechanisms are defined to yield the same curve, a discriminating test needs developmental measurements that have not been archived.

operationalization: Regress a curvature or spiral-tightness measure on basal horn diameter across antelopes, goats, and sheep, with a phylogenetic control. The claim is supported by a positive thickness–curvature relationship within and across clades; no relationship, or the reverse, would refute the stated tendency.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D bovid skulls from which basal diameter and centerline curvature can be measured together

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Additional specimens to widen the sample of slender and heavy horns

obstacles: Related species share both thick horns and strong spirals, so a naive correlation is phylogenetically confounded.
Scanned samples under-represent slender-horned antelopes relative to sheep and goats.
rationale: Thickness and curvature are ordinary measurements on horns that are already scanned or photographed, and a phylogenetic regression is standard. The open sample can test the tendency in the better-represented bovids and is not a balanced survey of every antelope. Shared ancestry can produce the same association Thompson attributes to the room a thick cross-section gives for unequal growth, so the geometric correlation is more resolvable than that mechanical reason.

operationalization: Score growth-ring waviness, cross-sectional ellipticity, and helical curvature on sheep, argali, antelope, and ox horns. The torsion account is supported if sinuous rings occur on non-circular, helically curved horns and are absent on cylindrical ox horns; sinuous rings on round horns, or smooth rings on strongly twisted elliptical horns, would refute the predicted association.

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs of horn sheaths on which growth-ring shape can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D surfaces for cross-section shape and helical pitch where the sheath or core is scanned

obstacles: Growth rings are a surface feature often missing from skeletal CT, and they are not a database field.
Seasonal growth and wear can wrinkle rings without torsion.
rationale: The predicted pattern is specific: sinuous boundaries on twisted non-circular horns, and their absence on cylindrical cattle horns. Photographs in museum portals show those rings for some species, but they have not been measured into an open table, and scans often stop at the bone. A scored sample could test the association, with remaining ambiguity between torsion and other causes of wavy increments.

operationalization: During circumnutation, compare epidermal or cortical extension rates on opposite flanks along the elongating stem. The claim is supported if the revolving bend is accompanied by a rotating excess of growth on the convex side over a long zone of the stem; it is weakened if the stem revolves while flank growth rates remain equal.
obstacles: Kinematic and local-strain measurements of twining stems are scattered in papers rather than held in one open repository.
Most series cover one or two model climbers, not twining plants as a class.
rationale: Unequal flank growth is a measurable alternative to uniform elongation, and classic and later experiments report it for particular twiners. Those measurements are not assembled as a public dataset a team could download and reanalyze, and they rarely span the diversity of climbing stems. The comparison with horn growth is an analogy; the plant data that exist can test local differential growth in a few species only.

operationalization: Grow matched twining stems on rough and smooth supports and measure torsion of the stem, adhesion, and bending stiffness. A mechanical couple is supported if twist appears with measured clinging on rough supports and disappears on smooth ones of equal diameter; an adaptive-rigidity account would require a stiffness benefit even where adhesion is absent.
obstacles: Darwin's smooth-versus-rough comparison is a narrative experiment, not an archived measurement table.
No current public dataset records stem torsion, support roughness, and rigidity together.
rationale: The contrast between rough and smooth supports is a clear experimental criterion and would separate a frictional couple from a general gain in rigidity. That experiment is not available as a reusable public dataset, and published accounts do not include the sample sizes and twist angles needed for a modern reanalysis. Resolving the claim requires new measurements or recovery of data that have not been deposited.

operationalization: Place landmarks on tine tips of paired antlers and fit a single ellipsoid or spheroid, allowing mirror symmetry across the midline. The claim is supported if one surface accounts for both antlers within a small residual and the tips lie on a continuous curve; systematically separate surfaces for left and right, or residuals that grow with tine length, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: CT and meshes of cervid skulls with antlers attached

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Photographs and records of red deer, wapiti, and other antlered species

obstacles: Many scans are of skulls after the antlers were shed, or of a single antler.
Open 3D coverage is good for a few deer species and poor for the rest of Cervidae.
rationale: Fitting tine tips to one mirror-symmetric curved surface is a direct test, and enough antlered skulls are publicly scanned to try it on red deer, wapiti, and similar species. That is the comparison Thompson invites, but it is not yet a family-wide sample, and shed antlers cannot test the paired surface. The analysis itself is a short geometric exercise once paired meshes are chosen.

operationalization: Fit logarithmic spirals and alternative curves to centerlines of claws, beaks, incisors, canines, and tusks, and test whether fit improves as the structure subtends a larger angle. The tendency is supported if long structures converge on a constant spiral angle and short ones are the same curve seen over a small arc; consistently better fits by non-logarithmic curves in long structures would refute the universal tendency.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D skulls, beaks, and teeth across vertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: CT of skulls and jaws for beak and tooth centerlines

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Specimen images that add claws and tusks poorly represented in skeletal CT

obstacles: Nails and claws are rarely CT-scanned compared with beaks and teeth.
Over a short arc, a logarithmic spiral, a circle, and a gentle bend are difficult to tell apart.
rationale: Skull archives already contain hundreds of beaks and teeth whose centerlines can be fit with standard curves, which is enough to test the tendency in those structures. The claim also covers nails, claws, and tusks, which are much less completely digitized, and it says the spiral is inconspicuous precisely when the arc is too short to identify. Existing scans can therefore accept or reject the law for elongated dental and rostral structures and only sketch it for the rest.

operationalization: Fit one logarithmic spiral to complete tusks of mammoths, living elephants, and American mastodons, allowing only a scale difference. The claim is confirmed if a shared angle fits all three once size is removed; species differences in angle, or a scale-free shape difference in pitch or taper, would refute 'the same spiral, only shorter.'

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Proboscidean cranial scans, often with the tusk base rather than the full erupted tusk

candidate_datasets.name: iDigBio
candidate_datasets.role: Museum records and images of elephant, mastodon, and mammoth tusks

obstacles: Complete tusks are heavy, often broken, and less often scanned than the skulls that held them.
A short arc from a living elephant underdetermines the spiral angle that a long mammoth tusk displays.
rationale: Equality of spiral parameters up to scale is a sharp comparison among three well-known tusk types. Public images and some scans exist, but complete, metrically usable tusks of mastodon, mammoth, and both living elephant species are not available as one open morphometric set. The short modern tusks are exactly the cases where a shared angle is hardest to estimate, so the test is possible on a small museum sample and not yet routine.

operationalization: Estimate divergence and parastichy families on elongated cones and on flattened capitula, then apply a geometric compression from cylinder to disc and ask whether one lattice reproduces both. The deformation account is supported if sunflower, thistle, teasel, and cone patterns are the same lattice on different surfaces; it is refuted if their divergence or chirality rules differ in kind rather than by surface shape.

candidate_datasets.name: Turing's Sunflowers
candidate_datasets.role: Counted parastichies and annotated images of 657 sunflower heads, the flat end of the proposed series

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Micro-CT of fossil conifer cones that preserve parastichy geometry on a steep cone

obstacles: Teasel and thistle heads are not in the sunflower count file, and open cone scans are few species.
A deformation can be drawn between many lattices, so the test needs matched divergence, not a visual resemblance.
rationale: The claim is that capitulum spirals and stem helices are one arrangement seen on differently shaped surfaces. Sunflower counts and images make the flat case measurable, and a few cone scans represent the elongated case, but the intermediate teasel and thistle forms are not in those files. A geometric mapping can be tried on this uneven sample; it would not yet cover the whole series Thompson lists.

operationalization: On annotated sunflower discs, measure the angle at which clockwise and anticlockwise parastichies meet at many radii. Isogonal intersection is confirmed if that angle is constant within heads and orthogonal crossing is uncommon across heads; a concentration of intersection angles at 90° would support Church's special case instead.

candidate_datasets.name: Turing's Sunflowers
candidate_datasets.role: Annotated seed-head images and parastichy counts for hundreds of Helianthus annuus discs

obstacles: The open images are domesticated sunflower heads, not a sample of other capitula.
Disordered regions of some heads do not define a single intersection angle.
rationale: Intersection angle is directly measurable on the annotated sunflower images already released with the citizen-science counts. Hundreds of heads are enough to estimate how often the crossing is orthogonal and whether the angle stays constant across a disc. Other inflorescences are outside this file, but the claim is aimed at the sunflower case Church discussed, and that case can be decided with the existing images.

operationalization: From primordia positions and plastochron, simulate the lattice produced by similar organs placed at equal intervals and compare it with observed helices and spirals. Agreement shows that regular production is sufficient to generate the pattern; it does not show that no further physiological process is involved, because auxin transport and mechanical buckling act by creating that regularity.

candidate_datasets.name: Turing's Sunflowers
candidate_datasets.role: Empirical parastichy lattices against which a regular-placement model can be compared

obstacles: Any mechanism that spaces organs evenly will satisfy the mathematical consequence Thompson treats as the whole explanation.
The denial of a 'further mystery' does not specify an observation that developmental models cannot also match.
rationale: Regular spacing of similar parts does generate helices on a cylinder and logarithmic spirals on a surface that includes the pole, and existing capitulum counts can illustrate that geometry. The same patterns are the output of later physiological models, so a successful geometric reconstruction does not discriminate Thompson's deflationary account from those rivals. The lattice prediction is testable; the claim that there is nothing further to explain is not decided by the fit.

operationalization: Count the conspicuous parastichy pairs on many cones per species, including Norway spruce and larch, and partition the variance within and among species. Constancy is supported if one pair dominates each species, such as 5 and 3 in spruce and 8 and 5 in larch; frequent within-species switching among distant pairs would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: A small archived set of cone CT scans with countable parastichies, not a multi-species survey

obstacles: Large published cone counts (pines, larches, spruces) are summarized in papers and are not one open raw file.
Cone size varies within species, which Thompson elsewhere expects to change the visible pair.
rationale: Within-species constancy of parastichy number is a straightforward count, and the examples are specific enough to check. The large samples that exist were published as summaries rather than deposited as specimen-level data, and open cone imaging covers too few species to replace them. A team could re-count a modest image sample, but the full species-level claim still depends on compiling scattered studies.

operationalization: Measure disc diameter on the annotated sunflower images and test whether parastichy pairs (34/55, 55/89, 89/144 and others) shift upward with size. The claim is confirmed by an ordered increase of both counts with diameter; it is refuted if pair identity is independent of size or if small heads systematically carry the higher pairs.

candidate_datasets.name: Turing's Sunflowers
candidate_datasets.role: Parastichy counts and annotated images of 657 sunflower heads, from which disc size can be measured

obstacles: The file is one cultivated species, whereas the claim also mentions other composite heads in passing.
Some heads are too disordered for a single pair to be assigned.
rationale: Size-dependent parastichy number is the pattern the sunflower study was built to capture, and both the counts and the images needed to measure disc size are public. Hundreds of heads span the Fibonacci pairs Thompson lists. Other composites are not in the file, but the stated example, and the scope centered on sunflower discs, can be confirmed or refuted directly.

operationalization: Treat the two chiralities of a parastichy system as a binomial outcome and test equality within species. Near equality is confirmed if the two directions are statistically indistinguishable, as in a recount near Thompson's 224 versus 243; a substantial and repeated excess of one handedness would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Turing's Sunflowers
candidate_datasets.role: Clockwise and anticlockwise parastichy counts on hundreds of sunflower heads

obstacles: The Norway spruce counts quoted in the text are not a deposited raw dataset and cannot be recomputed from the sunflower file.
A bias in one species would not by itself describe every phyllotactic system.
rationale: Handedness is recorded directly in the open sunflower counts, and a binomial test of equal direction is immediate. That decides the general claim of near equality for a large, single-species sample of the same kind of spiral system. The particular spruce tally is a historical count without a public specimen table, so the spruce example is not reanalyzable, while the broader chirality claim is.

operationalization: Given a single regular genetic spiral, the presence of one Fibonacci parastichy pair already fixes the lattice, and the lower pairs are alternate contact directions in that same lattice. Counting them on a cone restates the geometry; it does not distinguish the theorem from a rival empirical hypothesis.
obstacles: A system that violated the entailment would have failed the premise of one regular genetic spiral, not supplied an independent biological outcome.
Visible versus latent pairs depend on which diagonals the eye picks out, which is a drawing convention.
rationale: The claim is Tait's geometric result that one Fibonacci contact pair on a single spiral brings the lower pairs with it. Once a specimen is regular enough to have a divergence and one pair, the other pairs are the same set of lattice lines counted another way. Data can illustrate the arithmetic, and they cannot confirm or refute it without changing the subject to whether real plants are regular spirals.

operationalization: Infer the leaves-per-turn index t from parastichy pairs or divergence angles across cones and other shoots, and estimate the fraction of systems with 2 < t < 3. The prevalence claim is supported if that class dominates and the other observed series sit at t = 3, 4, or 5; a large share of systems outside those bins would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Turing's Sunflowers
candidate_datasets.role: Parastichy pairs for one capitulum type, convertible to a local estimate of t

obstacles: No open catalogue records t, or even parastichy pairs, across the vascular plants.
Sunflower heads are a high-Fibonacci subset and will overstate the share of systems near the golden angle.
rationale: The index t is recoverable from the parastichy pairs Thompson treats as ordinary observations, so the frequency claim is empirically sharp. The deposited counts that make the conversion easy are mostly sunflowers, which are a poor sample of 'the great majority' of cones and leafy shoots. Published cone surveys fill some of the gap only after compilation, so the global prevalence statement is only partly testable now.

operationalization: On cones or other lattices, measure divergence angle and the ratio of the diagonals of each scale's circumscribed rhomb, and predict which parastichy family is visually dominant. The claim is supported if that diagonal ratio predicts the conspicuous family when divergence is held constant, and divergence does not predict it when the ratio is held constant.

candidate_datasets.name: Turing's Sunflowers
candidate_datasets.role: Images of florets whose contact rhombs can be measured, in a system with limited shape variation

obstacles: Sunflower florets are similar in proportion, so they provide little independent variation in the rhomb.
Cone-scale proportions and divergence are not tabulated together in an open multi-species file.
rationale: The predictor Thompson specifies, the diagonal ratio of the leaf rhomb rather than the divergence angle, is a concrete measurement and yields an obvious comparison. Existing sunflower images let a team measure rhombs, but floret shape hardly varies, and the fir-cones where scale proportions do vary lack a public morphometric table. The test is well posed and currently limited to whatever images an investigator is willing to digitize.

operationalization: The continued-fraction limit of 1/2, 2/3, 3/5, … is an arithmetic fact about those fractions. Calling the limit biologically insignificant, and the precise divergence unimportant, does not state a measurement that would separate a coincidence from a developmental attractor, because both accounts produce the same sequence.
obstacles: Biological significance is not defined as a variable or a decision threshold.
A packing optimum, a dynamical attractor, and a mathematical coincidence can leave identical parastichy counts.
rationale: The convergence of those fractions to the golden mean is mathematics, and the further assertion that the convergence has no biological significance is an interpretation of that mathematics. Phyllotactic counts are compatible with the coincidence reading and with models in which the golden angle is an attractor of growth. No dataset outcome decides which reading is the significant one without an extra definition the claim does not supply.

operationalization: Tabulate phyllotactic fractions across leaves, cones, and capitula and compare the frequency of 1/2, 2/3, and 3/5 with that of 8/13, 13/21, and higher Fibonacci approximations. The claim is supported if the coarser fractions dominate the flora; it is refuted if close approximations are the common case outside large capitula.

candidate_datasets.name: Turing's Sunflowers
candidate_datasets.role: Frequencies of Fibonacci and non-Fibonacci parastichy pairs in sunflower heads, a high-order subset

obstacles: Sunflowers are enriched for the high pairs the claim says are rare, so that file alone cannot represent phyllotaxis across plants.
Leaf-arrangement surveys remain in botanical compilations rather than one open trait table.
rationale: Rarity of close golden-mean approximations versus abundance of 1/2, 2/3, and 3/5 is a frequency comparison with a clear alternative, the ideal-angle expectation that better approximations should prevail. The best open count file is sunflowers, where high pairs are common, so it tests the wrong end of the distribution for a flora-wide claim. Broader evidence is real but scattered, and a definitive cross-plant ranking would require a compilation that does not yet exist as a dataset.

operationalization: In a light-interception model, vary internode length and divergence angle over the ranges seen on leafy shoots and compare the change in mutual shading. The geometric claim is supported if realistic internode changes reduce overlap far more than realistic angle changes; it is refuted if, at observed leaf sizes, angle adjustments move exposure as much as internode changes do.
obstacles: Divergence angle and internode length are seldom published together as an open shoot-architecture table.
A larger geometric effect on exposure does not by itself show what the plant's developmental means of optimizing light are.
rationale: The comparison Thompson makes is a sensitivity calculation: separating leaves along the stem versus adjusting azimuth. Typical internodes, leaf sizes, and divergences are known from many studies, but they are not one downloadable shoot dataset, and the sunflower file does not represent leafy stems. The geometric inequality can be evaluated for published ranges with standard models; the adaptive conclusion that the ideal angle therefore cannot be the plant's means is a further inference.

operationalization: The claim concludes that the Fibonacci series, its supposed usefulness, and natural selection's role in introducing it deserve no place in botanical explanation. That is a decision about what belongs in a theory, not a result that a count of parastichies or a fitness assay would confirm or refute.
obstacles: Usefulness and 'a place in the study of botanical phenomena' are not defined as measurable outcomes.
Evidence that Fibonacci packing has a function would address a different claim from the one that the topic should be excluded.
rationale: Thompson's conclusion is a dismissal of a research program: the series, its utility, and a selectionist origin are to be left out of botanical explanation. Parastichy frequencies and packing efficiency can inform narrower questions about function, and they do not decide what deserves a place in the science. The statement as made has no distinguishing empirical consequence.

operationalization: Classify each egg by whether length exceeds width (prolate or spherical) or width exceeds length (oblate), using species-level shape measurements. The claim is confirmed if oblate eggs are absent across the measured hard-shelled eggs; a single well-measured oblate species would refute the universal negative.

candidate_datasets.name: Avian egg shape, oviduct, and pelvis
candidate_datasets.role: Egg length and shape indices for 955 bird species in 39 orders, sufficient to detect an oblate egg

candidate_datasets.name: Stoddard et al. 2017 egg-shape supplement
candidate_datasets.role: Asymmetry and ellipticity for about 1,400 bird species from nearly 50,000 eggs

obstacles: Both open compilations are birds; tortoise and crocodile eggs are a stated part of the scope and are not in these files.
Spherical eggs sit on the boundary and need a measurement-error rule before being called prolate.
rationale: Prolate versus oblate is read directly from length and breadth, and two large open bird-egg compilations already contain those measurements. An oblate bird egg would be visible immediately, so the claim is decidable for the animals that dominate the chapter. Reptile eggs remain outside the files, which limits the stated scope without preventing a clear test for birds.

operationalization: Regress egg asymmetry on egg size relative to adult body size across species, with a phylogenetic control, and inspect named cases such as guillemots, sandpipers, terns, and Apteryx. The common rule is supported by a positive relationship and by the stated exceptions having large oviducts; the pressure explanation is not tested unless oviduct pressure, rather than relative size alone, is measured.

candidate_datasets.name: Avian egg shape, oviduct, and pelvis
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level egg shape together with oviduct and pelvic measurements for a large sample of birds

candidate_datasets.name: Stoddard et al. 2017 egg-shape supplement
candidate_datasets.role: Asymmetry, ellipticity, and egg length for about 1,400 species, joinable to adult body size

obstacles: Relative size is a proxy for the pressure Thompson invokes, and flight or nesting correlates can produce the same pattern.
Oviduct dimensions in the open file are not pressure records along the forming egg.
rationale: The comparative rule, that the most tapered eggs are large relative to the parent, can be fit directly to open shape and adult-size data spanning most bird orders. Those same datasets have already been used to compare anatomical and incubation correlates, so the pattern is resolvable and the pressure mechanism is only proxied. A positive size–asymmetry slope would support the rule Thompson states and would still leave rival causes of taper in play.

operationalization: Within domestic fowl, compare egg mass and a roundness index between a pullet's first eggs and her later eggs, and among breeds that differ in relative egg size. The claim is confirmed if first eggs are both smaller and rounder, and if breeds laying smaller eggs relative to body size lay rounder ones; either association failing would refute the corresponding half.
obstacles: Cross-species egg tables collapse Gallus to a single average and omit laying sequence.
Breed and age series exist mainly as tables inside poultry papers and would have to be compiled.
rationale: The within-bird and among-breed comparisons are precise and, for domestic fowl, match the claim's scope exactly. The large avian datasets do not resolve a pullet's laying sequence or breed differences, so the needed numbers are scattered in the poultry literature rather than sitting in one open file. Discrimination would be high after a compilation, which is why the claim is only partly resolvable from what is already released.

operationalization: Record pressure along the oviduct during peristalsis and test whether the maximum lies behind the egg's midpoint, with the blunt end anterior. The pressure map would confirm the mechanism; a mid-egg or anterior pressure peak, or blunt-end-rearward travel as the usual case, would refute it. Inferring the pressure peak from the finished taper assumes the model under test.

candidate_datasets.name: Avian egg shape, oviduct, and pelvis
candidate_datasets.role: Egg asymmetry and oviduct size across birds; peristaltic pressure along the egg is not measured

obstacles: Open egg archives record the finished shape, not the pressure distribution that is supposed to have formed it.
Using taper to infer a posterior pressure peak repeats the hypothesis.
rationale: The mechanism specifies where peristaltic pressure peaks and which end of the egg is anterior. Comparative shape and oviduct dimensions are public, and they do not contain that pressure profile or the direction of the peristaltic wave. A shape model can be made consistent with the story, but confirming or refuting the stated pressure pattern requires physiological measurements that are not yet a dataset.

operationalization: Compare models that predict egg asymmetry and elongation from oviduct and pelvic dimensions with models that predict them from nest site and clutch arrangement. The anti-adaptation half is supported if nest variables add little once anatomy is included; the positive claim that radial oviduct pressure is the essential cause still requires a pressure measurement the anatomical sizes only proxy.

candidate_datasets.name: Avian egg shape, oviduct, and pelvis
candidate_datasets.role: Egg shape, oviduct size, and pelvic measures for hundreds of species, with incubation context discussed in the source study

candidate_datasets.name: Stoddard et al. 2017 egg-shape supplement
candidate_datasets.role: Asymmetry and ellipticity joined to life-history and flight variables for a nesting-adaptation test

obstacles: Oviduct diameter and pelvic size are not the radial pressure of successive annuli.
Flight-related body shape is a third correlate that can mimic an oviduct effect.
rationale: Open comparative files are sufficient to ask whether nest type accounts for egg form once female anatomy is considered, which is the contrast Thompson draws with adaptation to nesting. They measure oviduct and pelvic size rather than the varying radial pressure he calls the essential cause. The negative claim about nesting can be examined now; the positive mechanical claim is only proxied, and locomotion-related anatomy remains entangled with it.

operationalization: For measured egg profiles, solve p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P under an explicit constraint on tension and external pressure, and compare residuals with purely geometric oval equations. The physical equation is supported only if a constrained pressure and tension field fits and the unconstrained alternative does not; with T and p_n both free, essentially any axisymmetric egg can be made to satisfy the equation.

candidate_datasets.name: Stoddard et al. 2017 egg-shape supplement
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level asymmetry and ellipticity used to test a membrane model of egg shape

candidate_datasets.name: Avian egg shape, oviduct, and pelvis
candidate_datasets.role: Raw egg measurements and shape indices for fitting profile equations across birds

candidate_datasets.name: Biggins, Thompson, and Birkhead egg-shape data
candidate_datasets.role: Preston parameters and outline-derived indices for a smaller set of eggs, including pointed auk eggs

obstacles: Internal pressure and membrane tension during shell formation are not in any of the shape archives.
A free tension function can absorb almost any smooth profile, which makes an unconstrained fit uninformative.
rationale: Egg outlines sufficient to compute the two principal curvatures are available for most bird families. The equation also contains external pressure, membrane tension, and internal pressure, none of which are measured, and if tension and external pressure may vary freely the equation is the equilibrium condition of a membrane rather than a restrictive law. A test with predeclared constraints on those fields is feasible and only partly identifies the equation Thompson calls the equation of all eggs.

operationalization: Locate distortions, thin shell, and rupture sites on pointed and abnormal eggs and test whether they concentrate at the narrow end. The observable prediction is supported by a significant small-end excess relative to area; a uniform distribution, or a large-end excess, would refute it. Peak tension itself remains an inference from curvature unless local stress is measured.

candidate_datasets.name: Biggins, Thompson, and Birkhead egg-shape data
candidate_datasets.role: Outline methods and example profiles of pointed eggs, not a catalogue of abnormality locations

candidate_datasets.name: Stoddard et al. 2017 egg-shape supplement
candidate_datasets.role: Normal egg shapes from which the small-end curvature prediction can be computed, without defect coordinates

obstacles: Abnormal eggs and burst sites are not fields in the comparative shape datasets.
Collectors discard damaged eggs, so museum series under-represent the failures the claim is about.
rationale: The visible prediction is that irregularities and ruptures sit at the small end, where the membrane calculation puts the greatest tension. Normal egg profiles are richly measured, and the locations of abnormal features are not part of those releases; they appear as scattered notes and figures in the poultry and oology literature. Curvature can be checked now, while the defect prediction needs a compilation of abnormal eggs before it can be treated as a dataset test.

operationalization: Link egg-spine position to sequence-based clusters of the adults that produced the eggs. One mechanically varying species is supported if lateral- and terminal-spined eggs are intermixed within one genomic lineage; two species are supported if spine position tracks deep, reciprocally monophyletic groups corresponding to S. haematobium and S. mansoni. The moulding hypothesis can be examined separately from the species question only with ootype anatomy.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public sequences of Schistosoma haematobium and S. mansoni from identified adults

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Taxonomy: Schistosoma
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic backbone linking the named species to their sequence records and species diagnoses

obstacles: Spine position was historically part of the species diagnosis, so early morphology-only assignments are partly circular.
Ootype shape, the proposed mould, is anatomical description rather than a row in the sequence archives.
rationale: The claim denies that lateral versus terminal spines mark separate species and treats the spine as a mechanical variant produced in the uterus. Reference sequences of both named parasites are public and are tied to strains whose egg morphology is known, which is enough to test conspecificity without relying on the spine alone. Whether a funnel-shaped ootype moulds the spine is a narrower anatomical question and is not what the sequence data decide; the species claim itself is resolvable with existing genomic records.
